51188: Your answers fit the free-will response (Augustine in its roots, Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne): God values creatures who can freely love, and freedom makes evil possible. It explains moral evil well. Its weak points are natural evil and the sheer scale of some evils. Many combine it with soul-making or cosmic conflict to cover those.
51189: Your answers fit the soul-making view (Irenaeus, John Hick): the world is a place where humans grow from innocence to maturity. Pain makes courage, compassion and faith possible. Critics ask why some suffering crushes rather than grows people, and why infants and animals suffer.
51191: Your answers fit the warfare view (many church fathers, C. S. Lewis in parts, Greg Boyd): the world is in a war zone. Rebellious spiritual powers corrupt creation, and Jesus' ministry and cross are God's counter-attack. It explains why Jesus treated disease as an enemy. Critics say it is hard to prove and can make Satan too strong.
51192: Your answers fit process theology (Whitehead, Hartshorne, David Ray Griffin) or the related 'essential kenosis' view (Thomas Jay Oord): God cannot force outcomes but lures the world toward good and suffers with it. It removes the question 'why did God not stop it?'. Critics say it gives up the biblical Creator and any guarantee that evil will be defeated.
51194: Your answer fits the biblical and Jewish tradition of arguing with God: Abraham, Moses, Job, Jeremiah, and after the Holocaust Elie Wiesel. Protest takes God's justice so seriously that it holds God to it. It is a form of faith. Many in this tradition never resolve the question and still pray.
51195: How people have wrestled with evil and God
51197: Many lament psalms are attributed to David and his musicians, though the Psalter was gathered over centuries. They give Israel a worship language for complaint, from 'How long?' (Ps 13) to the unrelieved darkness of Ps 88. Dates of individual psalms are debated.
51199: As Babylon rises, Habakkuk asks why God lets the wicked swallow the righteous (Hab 1:13). God answers that the righteous will live by faithfulness (Hab 2:4). The prophet ends trusting God even with empty fields (Hab 3:17-19). Date approximate.
51201: The Babylonians destroy the temple. Lamentations mourns the city in five acrostic poems, admits sin, and also protests the horror (Lam 2:20). At its centre stands hope in God's steadfast love (Lam 3:22-23). It ends with an open question (Lam 5:20-22).
51203: The date of the book of Job is unknown; many scholars place its final form between the 7th and 4th centuries BC, while its setting is patriarchal. It is the Bible's longest treatment of innocent suffering.
51205: The Greek philosopher Epicurus (died about 270 BC) is credited with the dilemma: either God wants to remove evil and cannot, or can and does not want to. The form we know comes from the Christian writer Lactantius, centuries later.
51206: Jesus on Siloam and the blind man
51207: Jesus rejects the idea that victims of a collapsed tower or a man born blind suffered for special sins (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3). Within a few years he is crucified, crying the words of Ps 22. Exact year debated (about AD 30 or 33).
51209: Paul describes creation groaning in labour pains, the Spirit groaning in prayer, and nothing able to separate believers from God's love (Rom 8:18-39). Date approximate.
51211: In *Against Heresies* Irenaeus pictures humans created as children who must grow into maturity and likeness to God. John Hick later took this as the seed of 'soul-making' theodicy. Date approximate.
51213: In *On the Anger of God* (chapter 13), Lactantius reports Epicurus' argument and answers that God permits evil so that wisdom and virtue can exist. Date approximate.
51215: Augustine sums up his view: evil is the privation (absence) of good, entering by the free will of angels and humans, and God, being good, would not allow evil unless he could bring good out of it. Western theology followed him for a thousand years. Date approximate.
51217: Thomas Aquinas places the problem of evil as the first objection to God's existence and answers, following Augustine, that God permits evil to bring good out of it. He develops evil as privation and God as impassible.
51219: At the Heidelberg Disputation, Luther contrasts a 'theologian of glory', who calls evil good, with a 'theologian of the cross', who calls a thing what it is and finds God hidden in suffering.
51221: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz publishes *Essais de Théodicée*, from Greek words for 'God' and 'justice'. He argues that God chose the best of all possible worlds.
51223: On 1 November, All Saints' Day, an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroy Lisbon, killing tens of thousands, many in churches. European thinkers debate whether this can be 'the best of all possible worlds'. Voltaire writes a poem (1756) and *Candide* (1759).
51225: In David Hume's *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*, published after his death, the character Philo restates 'Epicurus's old questions' and argues that the world's mixed goodness does not point to a perfectly good designer.
51227: Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov tells stories of tortured children and refuses any harmony bought at that price. Dostoevsky answers through the characters of Zosima and Alyosha rather than an argument.
51229: J. L. Mackie's article 'Evil and Omnipotence' argues that the beliefs of theists are positively irrational. It sets the agenda for twenty years of philosophy of religion.
51231: Elie Wiesel's memoir of Auschwitz and Buchenwald appears in English (Yiddish 1956, French 1958). It records the death of faith in a God of easy answers and the question 'Where is God?' at the hanging of a child.
51233: John Hick publishes *Evil and the God of Love*, setting Augustinian and Irenaean theodicies side by side. Richard Rubenstein publishes *After Auschwitz*, rejecting the traditional God of history. Emil Fackenheim announces his '614th commandment' the following year (1967).
51235: Jürgen Moltmann argues that God suffers in the cross of Jesus and that only a suffering God can help. The book shapes modern theology of suffering (English 1974).
51237: Alvin Plantinga's *God, Freedom and Evil* argues that it is possible God could not create free creatures who never do wrong. Many philosophers come to regard the logical problem as answered.
51239: William Rowe's paper with the dying fawn shifts debate to the evidential problem: intense suffering that seems pointless makes God unlikely. Stephen Wykstra replies in 1984 with what becomes skeptical theism.
51241: Rabbi Harold Kushner's *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* argues that God does not cause tragedies and is not all-controlling. Millions of readers, Jewish and Christian, find comfort; many theologians object.
51243: On 26 December, a tsunami kills about 230,000 people across many countries, including thousands on the Tamil Nadu coast, especially Nagapattinam district. Christians, Hindus and Muslims ask why; churches and temples become relief centres. Many Christian leaders said publicly that the first responses must be grief, presence and practical help, not quick explanations.
51244: Texts, thinkers and events in the conversation
51245: Filter by colour group to see the biblical texts, the classic and modern thinkers, the Jewish voices, and the events and lives that shaped how people think about evil. Each card says what the person or text contributes and where it is questioned.
51246: A blameless man suffers, argues with God and is finally answered from the whirlwind.
51247: The prologue lets readers see what Job never sees: a heavenly scene in which 'the satan' (Hebrew ha-satan, 'the accuser', with the article, more a title than a name) questions whether Job serves God for nothing. Job's friends defend God by accusing Job. Job accuses God but keeps addressing him. God's speeches (Job 38-41) do not explain the suffering; they widen Job's view of a vast, wild creation that God governs. God then says the friends 'have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has' (Job 42:7) and asks Job to pray for them. Readers disagree whether the restoration at the end (Job 42:10-17) undercuts or completes the book's message.
51253: A lament that never turns to praise and ends with the word 'darkness'.
51254: Most laments move from complaint to trust. Psalm 88 does not. The psalmist has been afflicted since youth, feels cut off from God, and ends with friends gone and darkness as the only companion. Yet the whole psalm is addressed to 'the God of my salvation' (Ps 88:1). Its place in the Bible tells sufferers that continuing to pray in the dark is itself faith.
51258: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?', the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross.
51259: The psalm alternates between abandonment and remembered trust, then turns to praise as God answers (Ps 22:21-24) and ends with the nations worshipping. When Jesus quotes its first line (Mark 15:34), Jewish hearers who knew the psalm by its opening would hear both the cry and the whole arc. Jesus' cry was real anguish, not a performance.
51261: The nation protests that it suffers even though it has kept the covenant.
51262: Israel recalls God's past victories, then says: 'All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you' (Ps 44:17). It rejects the idea that the disaster is punishment and calls God to 'wake up' (Ps 44:23). Paul quotes verse 22 in Rom 8:36. Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust have often turned to this psalm.
51263: Psalm 73: the prosperity of the wicked
51264: Asaph nearly loses faith watching the wicked thrive, until he enters God's sanctuary.
51265: The psalm honestly states the problem (Ps 73:2-14), then finds a new view in worship: the end of the wicked, and above all the presence of God as the psalmist's portion (Ps 73:23-26). It does not deny the facts; it changes the frame.
51266: A prophet who questions God's justice and ends in trust without answers.
51267: Habakkuk asks why God tolerates violence in Judah; God says he is raising up Babylon. That makes it worse: how can a holy God use a more wicked nation? The prophet waits on the watchtower and receives the promise that the righteous will live by faithfulness. The book ends with a song of trust even if the fig tree does not blossom (Hab 3:17-19).
51268: Poems of grief after Jerusalem's destruction, with hope at the centre.
51269: The book admits Judah's sin but refuses to let that explain away the horror; it describes starving mothers and slaughtered priests (Lam 2:20). Its centre declares that the Lord's mercies are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23) and that he does not afflict from the heart (Lam 3:33). It ends with a question, not an answer. Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the fast for the temple's fall.
51271: Life 'under the sun' is fleeting; time and chance happen to all.
51272: The Teacher observes that the race is not always to the swift and that righteous people perish while the wicked live long (Eccl 7:15, Eccl 9:11). He refuses simple formulas but still counsels fearing God, enjoying God's gifts and remembering judgement (Eccl 12:13-14). The Hebrew word hevel ('vapour, breath') describes life's brevity and elusiveness.
51275: Jesus: those eighteen victims were not worse sinners than anyone else.
51276: People tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate. He raises a second case himself, a natural disaster: a tower that fell and killed eighteen. In both cases he denies that the victims were especially guilty, then turns the question back: 'unless you repent, you will all likewise perish'. Disaster is a call to everyone, not a verdict on the victims.
51278: 'Who sinned, this man or his parents?' Neither.
51279: The disciples assume a moral cause behind a birth defect, a view found in some Jewish teaching of the time. Jesus rejects both options and says the man's condition is an occasion for 'the works of God' to be displayed, and then heals him. The sentence is about what God will do, not a claim that God blinded him for a show; translators and interpreters debate the exact sense of John 9:3.
51280: Joseph: meant for evil, meant for good
51281: Two intentions in one event: the brothers' evil and God's good purpose.
51282: Joseph tells his brothers that they meant to harm him but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive (Gen 50:20). Reformed theologians read this as God ordaining the event; others read it as God redeeming an evil he permitted. Either way the text holds the brothers responsible and does not call the betrayal good.
51283: A 'messenger of Satan' that God did not remove, through which Christ's power was shown.
51284: Paul pleads three times for relief and receives the answer: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor 12:9). The text holds together Satan's harm, God's purpose (to keep Paul from pride) and an unanswered request. What the thorn was is unknown.
51286: Creation, believers and the Spirit all groan toward renewal; nothing separates us from God's love.
51287: Paul says creation was 'subjected to futility' in hope and waits for liberation (Rom 8:20-21). Believers groan too, and the Spirit groans in prayer (Rom 8:23-26). Verse 28 says God works in all things for good for those who love him; it does not say all things are good. The chapter ends with a list of real dangers that cannot separate us from God's love (Rom 8:35-39).
51289: The end of the story: God dwells with humans and death is no more.
51290: The martyrs ask 'How long?' (Rev 6:10). The book answers with judgement on evil powers and a new heaven and new earth where God wipes every tear and mourning and pain are gone (Rev 21:4). Many theologians say any adequate theodicy must look here, because only the end of the story can show whether evil is truly defeated.
51292: Evil is the absence of good, entered through free will; God brings good out of it.
51293: Augustine had been a Manichean, believing in two equal powers of good and evil. He rejected this: God made all things good, and evil is a privation, a lack or corruption of good. Sin began in the free choice of angels and humans, and the disorder of nature followed. His influence on Western theology is enormous. Critics ask how a perfectly good creature could first choose evil, and how a historical Fall fits with suffering in nature long before humans.
51295: Humans were made as children, to grow into the likeness of God.
51296: Irenaeus taught that Adam and Eve were created immature and that God patiently trains humanity toward maturity, with Christ recapitulating (summing up and restoring) the human story. He did not write a full theodicy, but John Hick named the 'Irenaean' type after him. Scholars debate how closely Hick's version matches Irenaeus.
51298: 'The best of all possible worlds' and its famous mockery.
51299: Leibniz (1646-1716) argued that God, being perfect, must choose the best possible world, and that the evils in it are part of the best overall whole. After the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Voltaire satirised the idea in *Candide*, whose tutor Pangloss keeps insisting that all is for the best amid disaster. Leibniz's actual argument is more careful than Pangloss, and some modern philosophers still defend a version of it.
51304: The protest of love against a harmony built on a child's tears.
51305: In *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880), Ivan collects true newspaper stories of cruelty to children and says he cannot accept any final harmony that requires them; he respectfully 'returns his ticket'. His brother Alyosha does not refute him with argument but answers with Christ's forgiveness and active love. Many theologians say this chapter is the strongest statement of the problem ever written.
51309: C. S. Lewis: two books on pain
51310: *The Problem of Pain* (1940) argued; *A Grief Observed* (1961) cried out.
51311: In 1940 Lewis defended free will, a fallen world and pain as God's 'megaphone to rouse a deaf world'. After the death of his wife Joy Davidman in 1960 he wrote a raw journal, first published under a pseudonym, describing God as a door slammed in his face, before slowly recovering faith. Readers value the pair because they show that the intellectual and personal problems are different.
51314: *Evil and the God of Love* (1966) and the 'vale of soul-making'.
51315: Hick argued that God created humans at an 'epistemic distance', in a world where God is not obvious and where real dangers exist, so that faith and moral growth could be free. He borrowed John Keats' phrase 'the vale of soul-making'. To deal with lives cut short, he relied on growth continuing after death and, controversially, on universal salvation.
51318: *God, Freedom and Evil* (1974): the free-will defence.
51319: Plantinga offered a defence, not a theodicy: he did not claim to know God's actual reasons, only to show a possible one. If creatures are significantly free, it is possible that every world God could create with free creatures would contain some evil (he called this 'transworld depravity'). Many philosophers, including atheists, came to accept that the strict logical problem had been answered. He extended the defence to natural evil by suggesting it could be caused by free fallen spirits.
51321: The fawn in the forest fire and the evidential argument (1979).
51322: Rowe, who called himself a 'friendly atheist', granted that theists could be rational. But he argued that intense suffering which seems to serve no good, like a fawn dying slowly and unseen in a fire, makes it likely that pointless evil exists, and so likely that God does not. His argument remains a central point of debate.
51325: Horrendous evils must be defeated within each life.
51326: An Episcopal priest and philosopher, Adams argued in *Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God* (1999) that it is not enough for God to bring overall good from evil. God must be good to each person who suffered, making their life worth living on the whole, finally through intimate union with God, who in Christ shared horrendous suffering. Her view leans toward universal salvation, which critics question.
51329: *The Crucified God*: God suffers in the cross of Christ.
51330: As a German prisoner of war, Moltmann found hope reading Mark's account of Jesus' cry of forsakenness. In *The Crucified God* (1972) he argued that the cross is an event within God: the Father suffers the loss of the Son, the Son suffers abandonment, and the Spirit brings life out of death. Supporters find this deeply consoling; classical theologians worry it makes God dependent on the world.
51332: Warfare theodicy: much evil is the work of God's enemies.
51333: In *God at War* (1997) and *Satan and the Problem of Evil* (2001), Boyd argues that the Bible's main framework for evil is a cosmic conflict with rebellious powers, and that Jesus' ministry treats sickness and oppression as the work of the enemy. He combines this with open theism. Critics, especially Reformed ones, think he limits God's sovereignty too much.
51335: God's power is persuasion; God suffers with the world.
51336: Alfred North Whitehead (*Process and Reality*, 1929) called God 'the fellow-sufferer who understands'. Charles Hartshorne (*Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes*, 1984) and David Ray Griffin (*God, Power, and Evil*, 1976) argued that the classic idea of all-controlling power is incoherent. Thomas Jay Oord's 'essential kenosis' is a related evangelical-leaning view. Critics say this God cannot guarantee the final defeat of evil.
51339: *Night*: faith wounded at Auschwitz, protest that never let go of God.
51340: Wiesel was deported from Sighet at fifteen; his mother, sister and father died in the camps. *Night* describes the hanging of a child and a voice asking where God is, and Wiesel's inner answer that God is there, hanging on the gallows; readers interpret this as the death of faith, as God suffering with victims, or as both. His later play *The Trial of God* puts God on trial. He remained an observant, questioning Jew.
51342: The '614th commandment': do not hand Hitler posthumous victories.
51343: Fackenheim, a rabbi and philosopher who was himself held in a camp in 1938, said in 1967 that Jews hear a commanding voice from Auschwitz: they must survive as Jews, remember the victims, not despair of the world or of God. The number adds one to the traditional 613 commandments of the Torah. Some Jewish thinkers object that no commandment can be added.
51345: Two radical answers: the God of history is dead; God gave up power.
51346: Richard Rubenstein (*After Auschwitz*, 1966) concluded that the traditional God who acts in history and chose Israel could not be believed after the Holocaust, though he valued Jewish community and ritual. Hans Jonas, in 'The Concept of God after Auschwitz' (lecture 1984), proposed that God, in creating, gave up power, so God did not intervene because God could not. Most Jews and Christians reject both, but both take the evil with full seriousness.
51348: *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* (1981).
51349: Kushner's son Aaron had progeria and died at fourteen. Kushner read Job as choosing God's goodness over God's total power, and concluded that God does not cause our suffering but helps us bear it. His pastoral wisdom (do not blame the sufferer, do not blame God for a world of natural law) helped many. Critics said a God who cannot help is not the God of the Bible.
51351: The natural disaster that shook the European Enlightenment.
51352: On All Saints' Day an earthquake, then a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon. Preachers called it judgement; Voltaire asked whether Lisbon was more wicked than Paris or London. Rousseau replied that humans had built crowded tall houses, so not all the harm was natural. The debate began the modern focus on natural evil.
51355: Natural evil on the Indian coast, and how faith communities responded.
51356: The wave of 26 December 2004 killed thousands along the Tamil Nadu coast, many of them fishing families, with Nagapattinam district hit hardest. Some explained it as karma, some as divine judgement, some as nature. Christian, Hindu and Muslim groups worked side by side in relief. The case tests the theodicies: none explain why these villages, and Jesus' words on Siloam warn against reading guilt into victims.
51358: A missionary in Tamil Nadu who wrote from twenty years of pain.
51359: Amy Carmichael (1867-1951) founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in Tamil Nadu to protect children at risk. After a fall in 1931 she was largely bedridden until her death. Her writings from that period, such as *Rose from Brier*, written for fellow sufferers, refuse cheap comfort and speak of accepting what God does not remove while trusting his love.
51362: Moral evil and forgiveness in Odisha, 1999.
51363: In January 1999 the Australian missionary Graham Staines, who had served leprosy patients in Odisha for decades, was burned to death with his two young sons by a mob. His widow Gladys publicly forgave the killers and continued the work. Her response did not explain the evil; it answered it with forgiveness, a costly act many Indians across faiths found moving.
